# Kuruṅgamigajātaka (Ja 206)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kuruṅgamigajātaka* (Ja 206), titled *The Antelope* in English translation, is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection. The story was delivered by the Buddha while residing at the Veḷuvana monastery near Rājagaha on the occasion of Devadatta plotting his assassination [Fausböll 1879]. Remarking to the monks that Devadatta had likewise attempted to kill him in a former life, the Buddha recounts the tale of the past opening with the verse *Ingha vaddhamayaṁ pāsaṁ* [Fausböll 1879]. In that life, the Bodhisatta was a kurunga deer dwelling in a forest near a lake, living in mutual friendship with a woodpecker (*satapatta*) and a tortoise (*kacchapa*) [Fausböll 1879; Cunningham 1879]. When the deer is trapped in a leather snare set by a hunter, the tortoise bites through the thongs while the woodpecker stalls the hunter with ominous cries; though the tortoise is briefly bagged, the deer draws the hunter into the forest to secure his friend's release [Fausböll 1879; Cunningham 1879]. In the story's conclusion (*samodhāna*), the hunter is identified as Devadatta, the woodpecker as Sāriputta, the tortoise as Moggallāna, and the deer as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1879].

 The narrative is widely represented in ancient Buddhist art, notably depicted in a relief on the railing of the Bharhut Stūpa [Cunningham 1879; Winternitz 1933], upon the gateways of Sāñcī Stūpa 1 [Karlsson 1999], and in the narrative programs of numerous temples of the Pagan period in Burma [Win Than Tun 2002].
